name: Michel Ney
summary: Ney defended Napoleon’s restored dynasty in the language of national acceptance, liberty and independence. His Swiss diplomacy combined armed intervention with reconciliation, civil sovereignty over former ecclesiastical rule, and protection of French commercial interests.

sources.title: Proclamation read by Marshal Ney to his troops, 14 March 1815
sources.author: Michel Ney; transcription held by the French Senate
sources.usedFor: His public justification for joining Napoleon and rejecting Bourbon restoration.

sources.title: Memoirs of Marshal Ney, published by his family, volume I (1833), especially pp. 8 and 29–30
sources.author: Michel Ney’s family; includes his correspondence
sources.usedFor: Own letter requiring punishment and restitution for military pillage; distinction between correspondence and family narrative.

sources.title: Memoirs of Marshal Ney, published by his family, volume II (1833), especially pp. 31–32, 142–152 and 164–167
sources.author: Michel Ney’s family; includes his correspondence
sources.usedFor: Swiss amnesty letter, St Gall sovereignty letter and personally conducted commercial negotiations.

sources.title: Ney’s Mission to Switzerland, 1802–03, Napoleonic Scholarship 6 (2015), pp. 93–108
sources.author: Wayne Hanley
sources.usedFor: Archival study of intervention, disarmament, detention, reconciliation and diplomacy.

sources.title: Ney to Wellington, 15 November 1815, reproduced in Papers concerning Marshal Ney, Commons, 14 February 1816
sources.author: Michel Ney; UK Parliamentary Papers/Hansard
sources.usedFor: His invocation of the capitulation’s protection against political prosecutions.

notes: The review covers revolutionary service, the Swiss mission, imperial campaigns, the Bourbon interlude, the Hundred Days and his final defence. The family-published memoirs are partisan biographies, not a continuous autobiography: correspondence is distinguished from editorial claims, and narrated actions receive medium confidence at most. Swiss federal policy devised by Napoleon, statements by Swiss negotiators, and the prosecutor’s allegations are not automatically Ney’s positions. Amnesty followed his earlier detention of opposition leaders. The proclamation is his delivered public position even though its drafter is uncertain. General appeals to liberty do not establish specific modern civil-rights or economic policies. All statement themes and remaining null answers were checked; no historical inferences were added. His objection to his own treason prosecution is not treated as opposition to capital punishment: an earlier letter pressed for enforcement of military death sentences.
